learn.intro: On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot in Sarajevo. Within six weeks the Great Powers were at war. This topic follows the July Crisis step by step and asks how the trigger set off the long-term causes.

blocks.p: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, visited Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, with his wife Sophie on 28 June 1914.

A group of young Bosnian Serb nationalists, armed with help from the Black Hand, planned to kill him. A bomb attack that morning failed. Later, after the archduke's car took a wrong turn, Gavrilo Princip shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie dead.
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and saw a chance to crush Serbian nationalism.

sections.title: 2. The July Crisis

blocks.p: Step by step, the crisis spread:

ul: 5–6 July: Germany gives Austria-Hungary the "blank cheque", promising support whatever it does.
23 July: Austria-Hungary sends Serbia an ultimatum with harsh demands.
28 July: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia.
30 July: Russia orders general mobilisation to support Serbia.
1 August: Germany declares war on Russia.
3 August: Germany declares war on France.
4 August: Germany invades Belgium (the Schlieffen Plan); Britain declares war on Germany.

blocks.p: The trigger was the assassination, but the long-term causes explain why a murder in the Balkans became a world war: nationalism created the crisis, alliances and the blank cheque widened it, and militarism (mobilisation timetables and the Schlieffen Plan) made it hard to stop. Remember Alphonse the Camel: the final straw was not the only reason for the collapse.

evidence: Blank cheque 5–6 July; ultimatum 23 July; Britain declares war 4 August 1914.

timeline.event: Franz Ferdinand and Sophie are assassinated in Sarajevo.
Austria-Hungary sends its ultimatum to Serbia.
Germany invades Belgium; Britain declares war on Germany.

questions.q: Describe two features of the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: What can you learn from Source A about why the July Crisis led to war?

sources.label: Source A
sources.provenance: A description of the ultimatum sent by the government of Austria-Hungary to Serbia on 23 July 1914.
sources.text: The ultimatum blamed Serbia for the assassination of Franz Ferdinand. It demanded that Serbia ban anti-Austrian groups and propaganda, sack officials named by Austria-Hungary, and allow Austro-Hungarian officials to take part in the investigation inside Serbia. Serbia was given only 48 hours to accept every demand.

questions.sources_note: Source A is described in our own words for revision practice. In the exam you will be given the source itself.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "The assassination of Franz Ferdinand was the main cause of the First World War." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh the trigger against the long-term M.A.I.N. causes and reach a judgement.
steps: Explain the role of the assassination.
Explain at least two long-term causes and how they made war likely.
questions.plan: 3 minutes planning, 15 minutes writing, 2 minutes checking.
mistakes: Agreeing completely with no long-term causes

full: P: The assassination was important as the trigger, but only to some extent the main cause…
E: For example, on 28 June… then…
E: However, this only led to war because alliances / militarism…
J: Therefore, the main cause was…
some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …

stretch.task: If the archduke's car had not taken a wrong turn, would war still have happened? Use the long-term causes to argue.
Which country do you think bears most responsibility for the July Crisis? Use dates as evidence.
Christopher Clark argued Europe's leaders "sleepwalked" into war. Find two moments in the July Crisis that support or challenge this.
Map every decision in the July Crisis. At which point could war most easily have been stopped?
